Moving investments into a TFSA: separate the market-value contribution, the cost and the gain

Four interactive charts follow a proposed in-kind contribution, unchanged gross market wealth, contribution room and the different treatment of gains and losses.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate a proposed in-kind contribution from its cost and room requirement

Interactive planning lab

Proposed contribution at fair market value$12,000
Positive capital gain before inclusion$4,000
Available room less proposed contribution$3,000

Original hypothetical CAD illustration of one proposed in-kind contribution from non-registered capital property to the same owner’s TFSA. Assume an eligible Canadian resident, a permitted qualified investment, verified allocated adjusted cost and independently verified available room across all TFSAs. Prices remain unchanged during the illustrated movement. No sale cash is received. Transaction fees, other contributions, withdrawals, non-residency, special property rules, inclusion rates, offsets, personal tax and future returns are excluded. A negative room remainder identifies a proposed contribution exceeding the entered capacity; it is not an executable plan or a calculation of legal excess tax. The tool does not automatically shrink the proposed transfer or establish eligibility.

The central idea

An in-kind contribution can use room and create a reportable gain without producing sale cash. Reconcile the contribution-date market value, allocated cost and verified room separately.

01

Start by identifying what is moving

An in-kind contribution moves an investment into a TFSA without first selling it for cash. It is still a contribution, and the investment’s account location is only one part of its treatment.

CRA’s current TFSA guidance treats a qualified in-kind contribution from a non-registered portfolio as a disposition at fair market value. That same value is the contribution amount. A gain must be reported; a resulting capital loss cannot be claimed.

The illustration assumes an eligible Canadian resident and permitted capital property, with no transaction expenses. Other registered-account transfers, special property rules and eligibility checks need their own analysis.

02

Follow the same asset through the two account locations

The original example proposes contributing 400 units at CAD 30 per unit, while keeping another 200 units of the same holding non-registered. The selected 600 units have a total market value of CAD 18,000 immediately before the movement.

After the proposed contribution, 200 units remain outside the TFSA with a value of CAD 6,000. The 400 contributed units have a value of CAD 12,000 inside it. The two parts still total CAD 18,000 at the unchanged price.

The stacked bars keep that conservation visible. The CAD 12,000 contribution is a movement of existing wealth. It is not another CAD 12,000 to add to the original CAD 18,000. Neither the transfer itself nor a statement’s contribution entry creates a cash receipt in this example.

This is a gross market-value comparison at one instant. It does not deduct any tax that may result from the deemed disposition, assign a value to future tax sheltering or assume subsequent investment growth. Existing TFSA assets are excluded from both bars equally.

03

Keep the allocated cost record beside the contribution value

The entered adjusted cost for the proposed 400 units is CAD 20 per unit, or CAD 8,000. At the selected CAD 30 market price, their value exceeds that cost by CAD 4,000. This is the positive capital gain shown before any inclusion-rate or personal-tax calculation.

CAD 8,000 describes the allocated cost record. CAD 12,000 describes the contribution-date market value. CAD 4,000 describes the difference. They answer separate questions and are not three independent assets.

CRA’s capital-gains calculation guidance distinguishes proceeds, adjusted cost base and disposition expenses. The zero-expense assumption is what lets this illustration use the simple difference above. Enter a verified allocated ACB, rather than assuming a displayed average purchase quote includes every relevant adjustment.

The tool accepts the per-unit cost as an external fact. It does not rebuild a pooled cost base, trace reinvested distributions, process corporate actions or select acquisition lots. Changing the number of units kept outside cannot change the cost allocated to the proposed contribution in this limited model.

04

A smaller market value can use less room without creating a usable loss

Change the contribution-date price to CAD 15 while keeping the 400 proposed units and CAD 20 allocated unit cost. The contribution falls to CAD 6,000 and the arithmetic loss is CAD 2,000.

The gain/loss chart shows that CAD 2,000 as a denied-loss magnitude. It does not show a negative tax bill, a refund or a loss available to offset other gains. At a CAD 20 price both gain and loss are zero. At CAD 30 the chart instead shows the CAD 4,000 positive gain.

These price rows are independent stress cases for the same proposed unit count. They do not describe a trading strategy, predict which price will occur or compare selling first with contributing later. Such a comparison would require its own dates, transactions and applicable rules.

A tax consequence also needs a cash plan. Here no sale proceeds arrive to pay a future bill. The calculator stops before tax liability because inclusion rules, offsets, other income and payment timing have not been supplied.

05

Test the market value against reconciled room at the contribution date

The default independently entered available room is CAD 15,000. Subtracting the CAD 12,000 proposal leaves CAD 3,000. Using the CAD 8,000 cost instead would incorrectly suggest CAD 7,000 remains, overstating this subtotal by CAD 4,000.

At CAD 40 per unit, the same proposed 400 units require CAD 16,000 of room. Against the unchanged CAD 15,000 input, the displayed remainder becomes negative CAD 1,000. The model keeps this failed proposal visible; it neither authorizes an excess contribution nor silently reduces the unit count.

The line chart fixes the room input while varying only the contribution-date unit price. In the default example, the two lines cross at CAD 37.50 per unit because 400 × 37.50 equals 15,000. That crossing is arithmetic, not a suggested order price or a guarantee that all records are complete.

CRA recommends tracking room from the holder’s own records; it applies across all of that person’s TFSAs and does not update immediately in the CRA account. Reconcile relevant transactions before relying on the entered capacity. The tool assumes that reconciliation is already complete and does not add an annual limit or calculate excess tax.

Retain the contribution-date valuation, unit quantity and allocated cost beside the updated room record. Those separate records make it easier to explain why the contribution, reported gain and remaining capacity have different amounts.
